title: Reading state: status, diff, and log
objective: By the end of this lesson you can answer three questions at any moment — what have I changed, what exactly did I change, and what happened before me — without guessing.

blocks.text: Most Git trouble comes from acting without looking. These three commands are the looking. They change nothing, they cost nothing, and running them before anything destructive is the single habit that separates confident use from cargo-culting commands off the internet.
status: where am I and what is pending

blocks.caption: The first thing to run, always
lines: git status
git status -s        # short form once you know the layout
# On branch main
# Changes to be committed:      <- staged, going into the next commit
#   modified:   app.py
# Changes not staged for commit: <- edited but not selected yet
#   modified:   README.md
# Untracked files:               <- Git is not following these at all
#   scratch.tmp

blocks.text: Those three groups map exactly onto the three places from the previous lesson. Reading them tells you what a commit right now would actually contain — which is usually different from what people assume.

blocks.caption: Two questions, two commands
lines: git diff              # changes NOT yet staged
git diff --staged     # changes that ARE staged — what the commit will contain
git diff README.md    # one file only
git diff main..feature-x   # difference between two branches

blocks.title: git diff --staged is the last check before committing
blocks.text: It shows precisely what is about to be recorded permanently. Reading it takes seconds and catches the debug print you left in, the commented-out block, and the credential you pasted in while testing.

blocks.caption: How to read diff output
lines: --- a/app.py        <- the old version
+++ b/app.py        <- the new version
@@ -12,7 +12,8 @@    <- location: old lines 12-18, new lines 12-19
def upload(file):
-    if file.size > 5_000_000:     <- a line that was removed
+    if file.size > 10_000_000:    <- a line that was added
raise TooLarge()

blocks.text: A modified line always appears twice: once removed, once added. Lines with a leading space are unchanged context, shown so you can see where the change sits.

blocks.caption: Reading history at different depths
lines: git log --oneline                 # one line per commit — the everyday view
git log --oneline -10             # last ten only
git log --oneline --graph --all   # the shape of the branches
git log -p app.py                 # every change ever made to one file
git log --since='2 weeks ago'     # a time window
git log --author='Malee'          # by person
git show a3f91c2                  # one commit in full: message + diff

blocks.title: The investigation pattern
blocks.text: A user reports that uploads started failing last Tuesday. git log --since='last tuesday' -- upload/ narrows it to a handful of commits, git show opens the likely one, and the question is answered from the repository rather than from anyone's memory. This is the same shape as reading a log file with grep, applied to code history.
Who wrote this line, and why

blocks.caption: blame is a question, not an accusation
lines: git blame app.py            # each line: which commit last touched it
git blame -L 40,60 app.py   # only lines 40-60

blocks.text: The name is unfortunate. Its real use is finding the commit that introduced a line so you can read its message and understand the reasoning — most often before changing something that looks wrong but was deliberate.

blocks.title: Read a repository you did not write
steps: Go to any repository you have (or continue in ~/git-lab)
Edit a file, then run: git diff       (what exactly changed)
Run: git add . && git diff --staged   (what a commit would contain)
Run: git log --oneline --graph --all  (the shape of it)
Pick a commit id from the log and run: git show <id>
blocks.expected: The pending state, the exact change, the staged change, the recent history, its branch shape, and one commit opened in full. Those six views answer nearly every 'what is going on here' question you will have.

cheatsheet: git status — where you are and what is pending; run it constantly
The three groups in status map to staged / not staged / untracked
git diff — unstaged changes · git diff --staged — what the commit will contain
In a diff, - is removed, + is added, a leading space is unchanged context
git log --oneline — the everyday history view
git log --oneline --graph --all — the shape of the branches
git log -p <file> — every change to one file · git show <id> — one commit in full
git log --since / --author narrow an investigation fast
git blame <file> — which commit last touched each line, so you can read its reasoning

checkpoint.prompt: You want to see exactly what your next commit will contain. What do you run?
checkpoint.explanation: git diff shows what is not yet staged. --staged shows the staged content, which is precisely what the commit will record.

checkpoint.prompt: In diff output, what does a line beginning with a single space mean?

choices.C: It is unchanged context, shown so you can see where the change sits

checkpoint.explanation: Only - and + lines are changes. Context lines are printed around them so the change is readable rather than floating.

checkpoint.prompt: Uploads started failing sometime last week. Which command narrows the search fastest?
checkpoint.explanation: Constrain by time and by path, then open the few candidates with git show. That is the whole investigation loop.

checkpoint.prompt: What is git blame genuinely for?

choices.A: Identifying who to hold responsible for a bug
choices.B: Finding the commit that introduced a line, so you can read its message and understand why it is that way
choices.D: Listing everyone who has ever contributed

checkpoint.explanation: It links a line to its reasoning. The most common use is checking why something odd-looking was done, before changing it and breaking whatever it was for.
